items.quote: may Abimelek be your joy, and may you be his, too!
items.contrast: the preceding reciprocal wish for joy versus the following curse involving fire
items.reason: The reciprocal wish immediately precedes the conditional call for fire. Answering only requires locating the adjacent earlier statement, not resolving a substantive relationship.

items.quote: as he approached the entrance to the tower to set it on fire
items.contrast: his specific purpose of burning the tower versus his broader action of attacking it
items.reason: The purpose clause explicitly states why Abimelek approached the entrance. The reader must distinguish his immediate purpose from the more general attack.

items.quote: Should I give up my fruit, so good and sweet, to hold sway over the trees?
items.contrast: giving up its good, sweet fruit as the cost of ruling versus the trees subsequently approaching the vine
items.reason: The fig tree's rhetorical question presents loss of its fruit as the reason it rejects rule. The following approach to the vine is an outcome of that refusal, not its cause.

items.quote: When the five men went into Micah’s house and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods
items.contrast: the five men taking the items first versus the priest taking them later as he joins the group
items.reason: The opening clause assigns the first taking to the five men; only afterward does the priest take the items and leave. The question tests both actor and sequence.

items.quote: “Please inquire of God to learn whether our journey will be successful.” The priest answered them
items.contrast: the priest as the person they address versus God as the source the priest is asked to consult
items.reason: The priest's answer identifies him as the addressee of the request. The reader must distinguish the human intermediary from God, whom that intermediary is asked to inquire of.
